teaser: To save this bronze, its maker threw his own dinner plates into the furnace.
review_notes:
Berlioz's opera Benvenuto Cellini (Paris, 1838) ends with the casting of the Perseus, with Cellini throwing his other works into the furnace: check wording.
Casting story (fever, clotted metal, about 200 pewter plates and dishes, toes of the right foot not filled) comes from Cellini's own autobiography, which is known to embellish.
Height of the bronze about 3.2 m; 1545 commission, unveiled April 1554.
The resemblance between Medusa's face and Perseus's face is a common observation, an interpretation.
Reading of the statue as a political warning by Cosimo I: standard interpretation.
Cellini says in his memoir that he killed men (his brother's killer, a rival goldsmith): to verify the phrasing 'more than one man'.
The black diagonal pole on the right of the photo is modern equipment, not part of the work; no spot points at it.
The carved heads at the corners of the marble base are described as goats (Capricorn was Cosimo I's emblem): check.
Base statuettes replaced by copies, originals in the Bargello: not visible in this photo, mentioned in text only.

lesson.text: Paris, 1838. On the stage of the Opéra, a sculptor runs out of metal in the middle of casting a giant statue. He orders every artwork in his studio thrown into the furnace. The mold fills, the chorus roars, curtain. The composer is Hector Berlioz, and his hero is a real man: Benvenuto Cellini.

The statue in that final scene is this one. It has stood in the same spot since 1554, under an open arcade on the main square of Florence, in rain and sun. The opera exaggerates, but not by much. Cellini told the story of that night himself, and he made sure it was a good one.

First, the subject. In Greek myth, Medusa is a monster with snakes for hair. Anyone who meets her eyes turns to stone. The hero Perseus gets close by watching her reflection in a polished shield, cuts off her head, and keeps it as a weapon.

lesson.title: One second after
lesson.text: Cellini picks the moment right after the blow. Follow it from top to bottom.

spots.title: The trophy
spots.text: Medusa's head, held up by its snake hair. Her eyelids droop and her mouth hangs open. Below the neck, thick ropes of bronze stand for the blood pouring out.

spots.title: Eyes down
spots.text: Perseus does not look at his prize. He lowers his gaze, calm, almost sad. The wing on his helmet is part of the magic gear the gods lent him.

spots.title: The body
spots.text: Medusa's headless body is folded on a cushion under his feet. One of her hands still grips her own foot, and on the right more bronze blood streams from the neck.

lesson.text: Compare the two faces again and you may notice something odd. The hero and the monster look alike: same straight nose, same full mouth, same heavy lids. Cellini's Medusa is no ugly beast. Some viewers see the pair as two sides of one being.

Cellini was trained as a goldsmith, a maker of jewelry, medals and table pieces. His most famous small work is a gold salt cellar made for the king of France. Before the Perseus, he had never cast a bronze statue of this size, and rival sculptors in Florence said openly that he would fail.

The man who ordered it was Cosimo I de' Medici, the young duke who had just taken control of Florence, a city that had long governed itself as a republic. A hero holding up a severed head on the public square was a message: this is what happens to my enemies.

Now, the night of the casting. Bronze is poured as a liquid into a hollow mold. Cellini wanted the whole figure of Perseus, about 3.2 meters (10 and a half feet) with its raised arm, cast in a single pour. The duke told him it was impossible: the metal would cool before it reached the head and the feet.

By his own account, Cellini was in bed with a raging fever when a workman ran in to say the metal had clotted. He jumped up, fed the fire with oak, and had all his pewter thrown in to make the bronze flow again: about two hundred plates, bowls and dishes from his own kitchen.

It worked. When the mold was broken open, the figure was whole, except for the toes of the right foot, which he had to add. Cellini spent years more chasing the surface, which means refining a cast with files and small chisels. He was proud enough to sign it, in a place no one can miss once they know.
Cellini's name is written in capital letters on the statue itself. Where?

spots.title: The strap
spots.text: The band crossing the chest carries raised Latin letters. You can read part of BENVENVTVS CELLINVS, followed by a word for “citizen of Florence.” The strap exists mostly to hold the signature.

lesson.text: A goldsmith's habits show everywhere. A sculptor used to stone thinks in big masses. Cellini thinks in ornaments: curls, feathers, tassels, a decorated sword. The slim, elegant body and the love of precious detail belong to the style called Mannerism, which preferred grace and virtuosity to plain naturalness.
The Perseus is a piece of jewelry enlarged to the size of a monument, and a technical dare: one enormous figure cast in a single pour.

The unveiling in April 1554 was a triumph. Florentines pinned poems of praise to the arcade, as was the custom. Cellini had also decorated the marble base with small bronze gods in niches. Those originals are now kept indoors, in the Bargello museum, and copies have taken their place.

spots.title: The sword
spots.text: A short, curved blade, held low and level. The action is over. In the myth the weapon is a gift from the god Mercury.

spots.title: Winged helmet
spots.text: The helmet, borrowed from the god of the underworld, makes its wearer invisible. Cellini turns it into a piece of fantasy armor.

spots.title: The sandals
spots.text: Straps and a small wing at the ankle: these sandals let Perseus fly. The foot presses down on Medusa's body like a hunter posing with his kill.

spots.title: A last grip
spots.text: Medusa's hand is clenched around her own foot. The body is twisted into a tight knot so that it fits on the small square base.

spots.title: Bronze blood
spots.text: A liquid, rendered in a hard metal: the blood hangs from the neck in wavy strands. In the myth, drops of this blood give birth to new creatures.

spots.title: The marble base
spots.text: White marble under dark bronze. Animal heads with horns project from the corners, probably goats: Capricorn was the personal emblem of Duke Cosimo.

lesson.text: Late in life Cellini dictated his memoirs to a young assistant. He boasts, settles scores, and calmly admits to having killed more than one man. The book stayed in manuscript for about 170 years. Once printed, it became one of the most read autobiographies of the Renaissance.

That book is why Berlioz wrote an opera, and why we know about the fever and the pewter plates at all. It is also a reminder to stay a little skeptical. The only witness to the most dramatic night in the history of bronze casting is the man who wanted to be its hero.

quiz.question: According to Cellini, what did he throw into the furnace to save the cast?
quiz.explanation: He says about two hundred pieces of pewter tableware went into the melt.

quiz.question: Where is Cellini's signature?
options: On the strap across Perseus's chest
On the blade of the sword
quiz.explanation: The chest strap carries his name in raised Latin capitals.

quiz.question: What was Cellini's original trade?
quiz.explanation: He was a goldsmith, which explains the love of fine ornament on the statue.

quiz.question: Which part of the figure did not fill with metal during the pour?
options: The toes of the right foot
quiz.explanation: Only the toes of the right foot were missing and had to be added.

quiz.question: What message did Duke Cosimo I want the statue to send?
options: A warning to his enemies in a former republic
quiz.explanation: A hero showing a severed head on the main square was a warning to opponents of the new duke.

quiz.question: Which composer put the casting of the Perseus on the opera stage?
quiz.explanation: Berlioz's opera Benvenuto Cellini ends with the casting scene.

facts.text: Perseus stares triumphantly at the head he is holding up.
facts.explanation: He lowers his eyes and does not look at Medusa's head.

facts.text: The Perseus has stood on the main square of Florence since 1554.
facts.explanation: It was unveiled under the arcade in April 1554 and is still there.

facts.text: The duke was sure from the start that the single pour would succeed.
facts.explanation: Cosimo told Cellini the metal would cool before reaching the head and the feet.
